name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,375

entries.clue: Clip of Hitchcock pitching for location of pilot (7)

indicatorNotes.Clip of: a clip is a short excerpt cut from a longer film, so the answer is a stretch snipped out of the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the director's name into the start of the next word

annotation.surface: A film clip of Alfred Hitchcock throwing a baseball, or pitching an idea to a studio.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clip' fits the film-director surface so neatly that it reads as movie footage; here it is the instruction to cut a run of letters out of the next two words.
annotation.definitionFit: The cockpit is the compartment where an aircraft's pilot sits, so 'location of pilot' is a plain descriptive definition.

entries.clue: Police eastern woodland (5)

blocks.note: cops is the everyday word for police officers
E is the standard abbreviation for east or eastern

annotation.surface: An instruction to police officers to patrol a stretch of eastern woodland.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Police' looks like a verb in the surface; it is the noun, and the plural slang for officers supplies the first four letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A copse is a small wood of trees or undergrowth, so 'woodland' is a straight synonym.

entries.clue: Repair scratched keel and prepare for action (5,3,5)

indicatorNotes.Repair: to repair something is to rebuild it from its parts, so the letters that follow are put back together in a new order

blocks.note: the thirteen letters to be rearranged

annotation.surface: A boatyard job: mend a keel that has been scraped, and get the vessel ready to sail again.
annotation.walkthrough: The nautical surface hides the fact that the answer is nautical too; 'Repair' sounds like shipwright's work but is only telling you to rebuild the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: On a warship the decks were cleared of loose gear before battle, and the phrase now means getting ready for any big undertaking.

entries.clue: Stiff old part for piano (5)

blocks.note: someone prim is stiffly formal and proper
O is the standard abbreviation for old

annotation.surface: A stuffy old piece of music written for the piano.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stiff old' reads as a description of the piano part; split it, and each word is a separate piece of the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: In a piano duet the primo is the upper part, played by the pianist on the right, as against the secondo below.

entries.clue: Handle land-worker (6)

blocks.note: a noun here: the lever a helmsman pushes to turn a small boat's rudder
one who works the soil by ploughing and turning it

annotation.surface: A job title: the person who handles the work on the land.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Handle' looks like a verb governing 'land-worker'; it is a noun, and the same word names both a boat part and a farmer.
annotation.definitionFit: A tiller is both the lever that steers a small boat and, literally, someone who tills the ground.

entries.clue: A party in outskirts of Sevenoaks returned drinks (5)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' puts the first pieces inside the next one
indicatorNotes.outskirts of: the outskirts of a town are its edges, so only the first and last letters of the word are used
indicatorNotes.returned: something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters run in reverse

blocks.note: the article is used as it stands
a do is an informal word for a party
the town's first and last letters

annotation.surface: Revellers heading back from a party on the edge of Sevenoaks with drinks in hand.
annotation.walkthrough: SEVENOAKS is a commuter town in Kent; only its two S's matter here. 'Returned' applies to A and the party, which flip before they go inside.
annotation.definitionFit: Sodas are fizzy soft drinks, so 'drinks' covers them as a plain plural.

entries.clue: Do well and draw in one of the best players, we hear (7)

indicatorNotes.we hear: what we hear is the sound of the words, not their spelling

blocks.clueFragment: draw in one of the best players
blocks.note: to suck is to draw in, and a seed is a top-ranked player in a tournament draw

annotation.surface: A tennis draw: a player does well and lands one of the top seeds.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Draw' pulls you toward the tournament draw the surface describes, but 'draw in' is breathing or sipping. Seeds are the players ranked highest so they avoid each other early.
annotation.definitionFit: To succeed is to achieve what you set out to, so 'Do well' is a straight synonym.

entries.clue: Carelessly I never rinsed last piece of plastic tableware (6,7)

indicatorNotes.Carelessly: done carelessly, a thing comes out in no particular order, so the letters are scrambled
indicatorNotes.last piece of: only the final letter of the next word is taken

blocks.note: the phrase to be scrambled
the last letter of the word, added to the mix

annotation.surface: A confession of sloppy washing-up: someone never rinsed the last plastic plate.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Last piece of plastic' reads like an item of crockery; it is just the final letter, the C that joins the twelve scrambled letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A dinner service is a matching set of plates and dishes for a meal, a particular kind of tableware.

entries.clue: Mollify supporter crushed by recent information from the south (7)

indicatorNotes.crushed by: something crushed by a thing is squeezed inside it, so the first piece goes within the second
indicatorNotes.from the south: in a down clue, read from the south means read upwards, so the letters are reversed

blocks.note: news is recent information
a golf tee supports the ball

annotation.surface: Soothing a fan who has been flattened by the latest reports coming up from the south.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supporter' suggests a fan crushed by bad news; it is the peg that holds up a golf ball. The reversal applies after the insertion, so the finished word is read bottom to top.
annotation.definitionFit: To sweeten someone is to soften them up or make them more agreeable, which is what mollifying does.

entries.clue: Translation of one Celtic epic shows creative expression (6,7)

indicatorNotes.Translation of: a translation renders the same material in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the thirteen letters to be rearranged

annotation.surface: A literary note: a translator's version of an old Celtic epic takes creative liberties.
annotation.walkthrough: Translators really do take liberties with epics, which is why the surface feels true; the translation here is of letters, not of language.
annotation.definitionFit: Poetic licence is the freedom a writer takes to bend fact or grammar for effect, a kind of creative expression.

entries.clue: Nobleman with medal in place of jewellery? (7)

blocks.note: an earl is a British nobleman
the OBE is a British honour, Officer of the Order of the British Empire, awarded as a medal

annotation.surface: A decorated aristocrat standing in a jeweller's shop.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface places a nobleman with his medal in a jewellery shop; the place is on the head, and the question mark flags that the definition is playful.
annotation.definitionFit: The earlobe is where earrings are worn, so it is a place for jewellery, defined by what hangs from it.

entries.clue: Key opening part of Olympic Games? (5)

blocks.note: E is one of the musical keys
a vent is an opening that lets air or smoke out

annotation.surface: Asking which ceremony forms the key opening part of the Olympic Games.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Key opening' reads as the grand opening ceremony. Split it: a musical key gives one letter, and 'opening' is a noun for a hole.
annotation.definitionFit: The Olympics are made up of individual events, the 100 metres or the high jump, so an event is one part of the Games.

entries.clue: Primarily sandy, arid, hot and rainless area (6)

annotation.definition: Primarily sandy, arid, hot and rainless area
annotation.definitionNote: An &lit: the whole clue describes the answer, while the same words supply its letters through their initials.

indicatorNotes.Primarily: primarily means first of all, so it asks for the first letters of the words that follow

blocks.clueFragment: sandy, arid, hot and rainless area
blocks.note: the first letter of each of the six words, in order

annotation.surface: A geography-textbook description of a scorching, rainless desert.
annotation.walkthrough: Every word earns twice: read straight it describes one famous desert, and its initials spell that desert's name.
annotation.definitionFit: The Sahara is the vast North African desert, as sandy, arid, hot and dry as the clue says.

entries.clue: Consequently allowed petition (7)

blocks.note: so means therefore, consequently
licit means permitted, the opposite of illicit

annotation.surface: A court's verdict that a petition was, in the end, allowed.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a legal ruling on a petition; 'petition' is really a verb, and 'Consequently allowed' is two separate words.
annotation.definitionFit: To solicit is to ask for something earnestly, which is what petitioning someone means.

entries.clue: Eggs reportedly expensive for some inhabitants of the countryside (3,4)

indicatorNotes.reportedly: what is reported is heard rather than seen, so the word is taken for its sound

blocks.note: roe is a mass of fish eggs
something expensive is dear

annotation.surface: A grumble that eggs are said to be pricey for country dwellers.
annotation.walkthrough: The price-of-eggs surface points at rural shoppers; the eggs are fish eggs, and 'dear' only has to sound right.
annotation.definitionFit: Roe deer are small deer that live wild across European woods and fields, so they are some of the countryside's inhabitants.

entries.clue: Scientist backing team working (6)

indicatorNotes.backing: backing means moving backwards, so the word before it is read in reverse

blocks.note: a side is a team
a machine that is on is working

annotation.surface: A scientist throwing his support behind a working team.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like support; it is the instruction to turn the team round.
annotation.definitionFit: Thomas Edison, the American inventor of the phonograph and a practical light bulb, is a scientist by the looser crossword sense of the word.

entries.clue: Supply safest meals (6)

indicatorNotes.Supply: read as the adverb of supple, supply means bendily, so the letters that follow are bent into a new shape

blocks.note: the six letters to be rearranged

annotation.surface: An instruction to cater the safest possible meals.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supply' is not the verb but the adverb from 'supple', pronounced SUP-lee; in a supple manner, the letters flex.
annotation.definitionFit: Feasts are large, lavish meals, so 'meals' covers them as a broader plural.

entries.clue: Boy starts to look everywhere for implement (5)

indicatorNotes.starts to: the starts of words are their first letters

blocks.note: a lad is a boy
the first letters of the two words

annotation.surface: A boy starting to hunt all over the kitchen for a utensil.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Starts to look' reads as the boy beginning his search; 'starts' is a noun here, the initials of the next two words.
annotation.definitionFit: A ladle is a deep long-handled spoon for serving soup, a kitchen implement.

entries.clue: Sanction me going back alongside British ship (7)

indicatorNotes.going back: going back means travelling in reverse, so the word before it is read backwards

blocks.note: the word is used as it stands
B is the standard abbreviation for British
the Argo was Jason's ship in the Greek myth of the Golden Fleece

annotation.surface: Someone asking permission to sail back beside a British vessel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sanction' can mean approval or its opposite, a penalty; here it is the penalty. The Argo is crosswords' favourite ship.
annotation.definitionFit: An embargo is an official ban on trade with a country, one of the commonest forms of international sanction.

entries.clue: Prohibits importing European foodstuff (5)

indicatorNotes.importing: a thing importing something brings it inside, so the second piece goes within the first

blocks.note: to prohibit something is to ban it
E is the standard abbreviation for European

annotation.surface: A government blocking imports of a European food product.
annotation.walkthrough: The trade-policy surface makes 'importing' sound literal; it just means holding a letter inside.
annotation.definitionFit: Beans are a staple food, so 'foodstuff' is a broad category that includes them.

entries.clue: Top dirty — covered with grease? (5)

indicatorNotes.Top: to top something is to cut its head off, so the first letter of the next word goes

blocks.note: soiled means dirty
the head letter removed

annotation.surface: A grubby, greasy top, like a mechanic's shirt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Top' looks like a garment in the surface; it is the verb meaning behead, which in a down clue lops off the letter at the top.
annotation.definitionFit: Something oiled has had oil or grease applied to it; the question mark allows the loose match of grease for oil.

entries.clue: Dog destroyed coke in parcels (6,7)

indicatorNotes.destroyed: something destroyed is broken apart, so the letters that follow are smashed and reassembled

blocks.note: the thirteen letters to be rearranged

annotation.surface: A sniffer dog at customs wrecking packages to reach cocaine hidden inside.
annotation.walkthrough: The drug-bust surface suggests a sniffer dog tearing open packages; the thing destroyed is the letters, 'in' included.
annotation.definitionFit: A cocker spaniel is a breed of small gundog with long silky ears, so 'Dog' is a definition by category.

entries.clue: Weapon is part of Beretta series (5)

indicatorNotes.is part of: the answer is only a part of the words that follow, a run of letters inside them

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the gun maker's name into the start of the next word

annotation.surface: A catalogue note that a gun belongs to one of Beretta's model lines.
annotation.walkthrough: BERETTA is an Italian firearms maker, which makes the surface's weapon look like a pistol; the one in the answer is electric.
annotation.definitionFit: A Taser is a stun gun that fires wired darts to deliver an electric shock, so it is a weapon.

entries.clue: Hold up South American writer before introduction to DC (7)

indicatorNotes.introduction to: the introduction to something is its opening, so only the first letter is taken

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for south
US stands for the United States, so for American
a pen is the thing that writes
the first letter of DC

annotation.surface: A South American author delaying a trip until after arriving in Washington, DC.
annotation.walkthrough: 'South American writer' reads as one novelist from that continent; split it, three words give three pieces, and the writer is a pen, not a person.
annotation.definitionFit: To hold something up is to delay or halt it, and to suspend is to put it on hold, so the two mean the same.
